article_title: Nearly Three Years After Apple Opened iOS to Non-WebKit Engines, Mozilla Says None Has Shipped Because the Terms Are Unworkable
summary: Automated checks passed; manual review found one hallucinated-verbatim quote and one overgeneralized technical specific, both subordinate to the lead and recoverable via a corrections note.

findings.message: Source fetched via Archive.org fallback (original returned 200)
Opening sentence attributes a quoted string to TechCrunch that is not verbatim in the source.
findings.details: Article text: "'all third-party browsers on iOS must use Apple's WebKit engine,' according to TechCrunch." The TechCrunch snapshot (source-4.html.gz) contains no such sentence; its actual wording is 'Currently Apple mandates third party browsers use WebKit, the same browser engine that underpins its own Safari browser.' The underlying fact is accurate and supported by that sentence, but the quotation marks present a paraphrase as a verbatim quote. This survived the writer's two self-reported verification passes.

findings.message: The 'fifteen calendar days' update requirement is generalized to 'any alternative engine' but Apple's source scopes it only to the Embedded Browser Engine Entitlement.
findings.details: Article text (Background, 3rd paragraph): 'Apple also requires that any alternative engine ... ship an updated app within fifteen calendar days of a new engine version ... according to Apple.' In the Apple snapshot (source-2.html.gz), the fifteen-calendar-day requirement appears only under the h5 'Additional requirements' subsection nested under the h2 'Embedded Browser Engine Entitlement' (in-app browsing / WebView-style embedding) — it does not appear under the 'Web Browser Engine Entitlement' section (full browser apps, the category a Gecko-based Firefox would use). The 90%/80% test-suite thresholds and the 30-day active-exploit mitigation window ARE stated in both entitlement sections and are correctly generalized; only the 15-day clause is entitlement-specific and was overgeneralized.

content_preview.title: Nearly Three Years After Apple Opened iOS to Non-WebKit Engines, Mozilla Says None Has Shipped Because the Terms Are Unworkable
content_preview.summary: Mozilla says that despite EU and Japan rules letting rivals bring their own browser engines to iOS, no non-WebKit browser has launched because Apple's compliance terms remain impractical.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Background

As of January 2024, "all third-party browsers on iOS must use Apple's WebKit engine," according to [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2024/01/26/apple-dma-webkit/), regardless of what engine the same browser uses on other platforms. That changed on paper that same month, when Apple announced iOS changes ahead of the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) enforcement deadline of March 7, 2024, according to [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2024/01/26/apple-dma-webkit/). Starting with iO...

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured Analysis (Background / Current situation / Implications), neutral tone, no editorializing or AI self-reference. Facts (regulatory timeline, Apple's published terms) are kept separate from the two sources' interpretive framing, which is itself clearly attributed rather than adopted as the Herald's own voice.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 5 snapshots read in full from local gzip snapshots in sources/2026-11/nearly-three-years-after-apple-opened-ios-to-non-webkit-engines-mozilla-says-none-has-shipped-because-the-terms-are-unworkable/. sha256 of each decompressed file was independently recomputed and matched the manifest for all 5 (source-0 through source-4); no tampering. manifest.json shows no suspicious_patterns on any source. source-0.html.gz (blog.mozilla.org, Mozilla's 'Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS,' Nov 20 2026) — read in full; confirms the central absence claim ('not one developer has been able to launch a non-WebKit browser on iOS,' 'Nearly three years since Apple introduced these conditions in the EU and almost a year since Japan') and all 8 direct quotes attributed to Mozilla in the article body verified verbatim (character-for-character, aside from straight vs. curly apostrophes), including the 'can't simply update,' 'second Firefox,' 'trap door,' and 'last major browser engine' lines. source-1.html.gz (heise.de, 'Mozilla is frustrated: Why iOS still has no real Firefox,' Nov 20 2026, status 200, fetched directly not via archive) — read in full; the two quotes attributed to heise ('neither platform has a browser with its own engine to this day; Apple's WebKit remains the sole engine under the hood' and 'since iOS 26.2 — on paper') both verified verbatim. Confirms 'nearly three years' for the EU DMA timeline and 'December 2025' for Japan's law, consistent with Mozilla and CSIS. heise's own reporting draws heavily on Mozilla's blog post but independently adds the iOS 26.2 Japan detail not present in Mozilla's post, so treating it as an independent confirming outlet is reasonable. source-2.html.gz (developer.apple.com, Apple's alternative-browser-engines support page, status 200) — read in full, including raw HTML heading structure. Confirms the EU-only distribution restriction, the iOS 17.4/iPadOS 18 minimum (verbatim quote verified), the 90% WPT / 80% Test262 thresholds (present identically under both the Web Browser Engine Entitlement and Embedded Browser Engine Entitlement headings, so the article's generalization to 'any alternative engine' is correct for this requirement), and the 30-day active-exploit mitigation commitment (also present in both entitlement sections). However, the fifteen-calendar-day app-update requirement the article also generalizes to 'any alternative engine' is, per the raw HTML (h5 'Additional requirements' nested only under h2 'Embedded Browser Engine Entitlement', line ~1223), scoped specifically to the Embedded entitlement (in-app/WebView browsing), not the Web Browser Engine Entitlement a standalone browser like a hypothetical Gecko-based Firefox would use — flagged as a finding above. source-3.html.gz (csis.org via Archive.org fallback, live URL returned 200 per manifest but archive_fallback:true was still recorded; Wayback capture dated 2026-11-16) — read in full; confirms MSCA took effect December 18, 2025, designating Apple, Google and iTunes K.K. as regulated providers, and the quoted phrase 'consumer access to alternative browsers and search engines' verified verbatim. source-4.html.gz (techcrunch.com, 'A closer look at Apple's browser-related changes to iOS in EU,' Jan 26 2024, status 200) — read in full. Confirms iOS 17.4, the March 7 2024 DMA deadline, the EU-only distribution restriction, and Mozilla's on-the-record 2024 objection (quoted in the source as 'extremely disappointed with Apple's proposed plan to restrict the newly-announced BrowserEngineKit to EU-specific apps'). The article's opening quoted sentence attributed to TechCrunch ('all third-party browsers on iOS must use Apple's WebKit engine') is NOT verbatim in this source — flagged as a finding above; the underlying fact is accurate (source: 'Currently Apple mandates third party browsers use WebKit...') but the quotation marks overstate verbatim-ness. Separately, this source also contains an extended set of quotes from independent researcher Lukasz Olejnik; none of those quotes, nor his name, appear anywhere in the final submitted article body — confirmed by direct string search ('Olejnik', 'researcher', 'consultant', 'Philosophy of Cybersecurity' all absent from body_markdown). The writer's reported decision to drop an Olejnik quote after two WebFetch passes produced conflicting 'verbatim' text held up: the quote is genuinely absent, not merely reworded. Anthropic disclosure: not required - the article concerns Apple, Mozilla, the DMA and Japan's MSCA; Anthropic is not mentioned and is not the subject.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Central claim (zero non-WebKit browsers shipped on iOS in ~3 years in the EU, ~1 year in Japan) is independently verified against both Mozilla's and heise's raw text and both state it in almost identical substance; this appears in the headline and lead and is solid. Two subordinate specifics do not hold up to a literal quote-by-quote and scope check: (1) the opening 'all third-party browsers...' string is a paraphrase dressed as a verbatim TechCrunch quote, and (2) the fifteen-calendar-day update window is generalized to 'any alternative engine' when Apple's own documentation scopes it to the Embedded Browser Engine Entitlement only. Both are in the Background section, not the headline, summary, or lead, and both are correctable with a short, specific public note. I verified the writer's self-reported second quote-verification pass did catch and fix the quotes it claims to have fixed (all 8 Mozilla/heise/Apple/CSIS quotes I checked verbatim are clean), but it did not catch this one TechCrunch misquote — the second pass improved the piece but was not exhaustive.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral throughout. Apple's compliance-terms criticism is consistently and correctly attributed to Mozilla's and heise's own characterization ('Mozilla framed...', 'Mozilla's summary verdict was put plainly...', 'Heise noted that this criticism...') rather than stated as the Herald's own conclusion anywhere in the body.
editor_notes.originality: No prior Machine Herald article covers this topic. Several November 2026 articles mention WebKit/Safari (betas, Ladybird, HomeView guidance) but none concern DMA/MSCA browser-engine-entitlement compliance or Mozilla's shipped-browser complaint; this is a new angle, not a duplicate.
concerns: Opening sentence presents a paraphrase as a verbatim TechCrunch quote ('all third-party browsers on iOS must use Apple's WebKit engine'); the underlying fact is accurate but the quotation marks are inaccurate.

The fifteen-calendar-day app-update requirement is generalized to 'any alternative engine' in the Background section when Apple's documentation scopes it specifically to the Embedded Browser Engine Entitlement, not the Web Browser Engine Entitlement a standalone browser would use.
recommendations: Future submissions should run a scope check on multi-section regulatory/policy documents (which requirement attaches to which entitlement/tier) in addition to a literal quote check, since an accurate-sounding generalization can smuggle in a scope error that a pure quote-by-quote pass won't catch.
editor_notes.analysis_requirements: Category is Analysis: word count 923 (within 800-2000). 5 sources cited, 3 independent of the subject (heise, CSIS, TechCrunch — all independent news/research outlets; Mozilla is the complainant/subject and Apple's own developer documentation is the subject being examined, so neither counts as independent), exceeding the 2-independent minimum. The article examines a 3-year regulatory compliance pattern across two jurisdictions rather than recapping a single release, and separates sourced fact (Background/Current situation) from each outlet's framing (Implications) — meets the Analysis bar.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Substantively solid Analysis piece: the headline and lead's central claim (no non-WebKit iOS browser has shipped in ~3 years EU / ~1 year Japan) is independently corroborated by both Mozilla's and heise's raw text, Apple's own criticized terms are accurately summarized in the main, Apple's-terms criticism is properly attributed to Mozilla/heise rather than stated as Herald opinion, and the dropped Olejnik quote genuinely does not appear in the final text. Two subordinate issues in the Background section — a paraphrase presented as a verbatim TechCrunch quote, and an entitlement-specific requirement generalized to 'any alternative engine' — are each a single recoverable specific, not a pattern, and neither touches the headline, summary, or lead, so APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS rather than REJECT. Featured candidacy: 1 - solid, well-sourced regulatory analysis for a developer/policy-literate audience, but a restated complaint rather than a new enforcement development, so not broad-audience or exceptional.
